doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Benny Goodman, Sicilian prejudice and Grandpa Mancuso
summary: On Goodman and Teddy Wilson, Mancuso links Sicilian experience of prejudice to jazz, and tells how his grandfather heckled his coach.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And here’s a statement you have regarding Benny Goodman. “That Goodman was white and more palatable to the dominant white pop audience should be of little surprise. Even while making a radical shift popular culture seizes upon that which is most accommodating and secure.”

Yeah. Well I think that was part of the culture at the time you know. That’s all. But you know, he brazenly went ahead and he brought in Teddy Wilson. You know, it helped that John was pushing, Hammond was pushing him all the time. But he was a Jewish guy. So he understood it a little better. I always felt that Sicilians understood that stuff too. Because we were swarthy and dark and curly-haired, my people. You know, we had been run over and run by all these other people, which I didn’t know at the time, but when my mother wouldn’t allow us to speak Italian, she said, “Trust me, I know why I’m doing it.” Because when she came up, her father, they used to make fun. And he was from the

northern part. Grandpa Giorlamo. They would make fun of him. Oh, you know, where’s your accordion? Where’s your Neapolitan hat? You people smell funny. You do all that. Oh yeah. It was not so nice. And with Sicilians it was worse. It was worse because the Sicilians had an attitude. You know they were run over by the Swedish — the Swedish folks came down and ran the country. And that’s when they had Godfathers. I mean I don’t approve of any of that stuff, but — and I got stories you see, from my grandfather Mancuso. He was one tough SOB. I didn’t like him at first. But he’d go to the ballgames and I’d have like maybe 33 points against — I’ll never forget it — against Fredonia, and I had a cousin who was going to be playing in another year, he was a freshman — at 33, at home, and there was nine minutes to go. And he took me out and wanted one of my other pals to play. And my grandfather would sit behind the back of the coach and he’d get up, “What are you doing taking the kid out? You don’t want him to score too many points, huh, he’s Sicilian. You white son-of-a-bitch.” I’d go, grandpa, grandpa, what are you — calm down. “You could have had 45 points.”
